question.choice1: The function has no vertical asymptotes
question.explanation:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} f(x) &= \dfrac {x^2-1}{x^4-1}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac {x^2-1}{(x^2-1)(x^2+1)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac {(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+1)(x^2+1)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\cancel{(x-1)(x+1)}}{\cancel{(x-1)(x+1)}(x^2 + 1)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac { 1}{x^2 + 1} \end{align*}

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

\[ x^2 + 1 = 0 \] This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

example.title: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes With Common Factors When the Denominator Has Complex Roots

question.explanation:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get \begin{align} f(x) &=\dfrac{x-1}{x^3-2x^2+3x}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{x-1}{x(x^2-2x+3)}. \end{align}

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

\[ x(x^2-2x+3) = 0. \]

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

  • Solving $x=0$ gives the solution $x=0.$

  • The equation $x^2-2x+3 = 0$ has no real solutions because the discriminant $\mathcal D$ is negative: \begin{align*} \mathcal{D} & = b^2 - 4ac\\[3pt] & = (-2)^2 - 4(1)(3)\\[3pt] & = 4 - 12\\[3pt] & = -8 \end{align*}

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is $x=0.$

example.title: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes When the Denominator Has Complex Roots

question.explanation:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= \dfrac{x^2 -9}{2x^3-2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{2(x^3-1)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^2-3^2}{2(x^3-1^3)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)}{2(x-1)(x^2 + x + 1)}. \end{align*}

Notice that we used the difference of cubes formula to factor the denominator.

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives \[ (x-1)(x^2+x+1) = 0. \]

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

  • Solving $(x-1) = 0$ gives the solution $x=1.$

  • The equation $x^2+x+1 = 0$ has no real solutions because the discriminant $\mathcal D$ is negative: \begin{align*} \mathcal{D} & = b^2 - 4ac\\[5pt] & = 1^2 - 4(1)(1)\\[5pt] & = 1 - 4\\[5pt] & = -3 \end{align*}

Therefore, the vertical asymptote is $x=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$
